extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and practitioners in patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Index and substantive rules covering patentability, inventive act/skill, inventor rights, claims/identity, letters-patent, joinder, licenses, jurisdiction, judgments, amendment/reissue, and related procedural and substantive patent-law standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention — definition and patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every new thing is patentable; must be the product of inventive skill; may be an art or an instrument; must produce physical effects; not a principle, a function, or an effect; substance of the invention includes whatever is needed to perform its function; form includes whatever is not needed to perform its function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essence is indicated by the want it satisfies; three groups — a force applied, a mode of application, a specific treatment of a specific object; whether an art or instrument is a means not an end; does not cover ideas not perceived by inventor; none made unless inventor comprehends it and can reproduce it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention — abstract vs concrete and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract and concrete distinguished; unity of invention; principal and subordinate are distinct units; an invention may, as a concrete art or instrument, express different ideas of means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception, perceiving a want and experimenting to relieve it, or merely thinking an idea that something could be done, is not complete invention until reduced to practice; reduced to practice only when actually practised; joint and several inventions may be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is a question of priority; priority is shown by use, publication, or patent; abandoned and forgotten use is not prior use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before 1886 patentable only if new to whole world; since 1836 patentable if new in United States; priority and date on question of priority are key to novelty; priority proven by publication/use/patent; future rights not assignable although contracted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (usefulness) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility must be present; utility absent when invention is immoral or very dangerous or impracticable; invention will not answer its purpose if lacking utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duty to put invention into practical use; not patentable if abandoned to the public; once abandoned can never be recalled; utility is relevant to novelty and entitlement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Only certain classes are patentable; classification of inventions in the Patent Office; what may be covered by a patent is determined by statutory classes and office practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invention to be treated as an art if possible; may be a vendible substance, an art, or an instrument; classification impacts joinder and scope determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and best form requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must disclose and define the invention accurately in the letters-patent and must disclose the best form of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor bound to good faith and reasonable diligence in disclosure; must comprehend and be able to describe invention — 'cannot have invented what he cannot describe'; all forms are covered by patent; patent must enable communication to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception and reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is a mental act; invention not complete until reduced to practice; reduced to practice is only when actually practised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception consists of perceiving the idea; reduction (physical part) is necessary; order of ideas (primary idea, function, means) matters; continuous process from conception to reduction; tests of when performed and how proved are substantive evidentiary inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive act — nature and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive act has two parts — mental (conception) and physical (reduction); it employs creative not imitative faculties and consists of discovery and construction; it generates a new union of the force, the object, and the mode of application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both conception and perception are necessary; inventive act produces a complete practical idea; scientific principles need not be perceived; may be instantaneous or prolonged, accidental or intentional; inventor must be able to communicate his idea to others for the act to be complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive skill (standard and proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive skill is defined as creative skill distinct from mere industry, judgment, or reflection; it is a question of fact for the jury and is distinct from novelty and utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of inventive skill is immaterial; may exist though the advance is slight; shown by utility, by prior unsuccessful efforts of others, by many steps to reach result, and sometimes by oath of inventor if legal novelty exists; presumed from the patent unless contrary proved; burden of proof rules and judicial notice of lack of skill are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor — rights, duties, and entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor is entitled to the exclusive practice of the invention, to the reward from the public under patent privilege, and to protection of his property in the invention; he must disclose the best form, act in good faith, apply for patent if living, and may assign or will his right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor creates the means, not merely perceives the end; need not comprehend scientific principles unless invention consists of them; may employ others to reduce to practice; rights of deceased inventors pass to representatives; inventor's obligations include reasonable diligence in disclosure and putting invention into use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership, joint inventors, and joint patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint invention may arise by community of mental effort or community of experiment; joint inventors require joint patent — sole patent for joint invention is void; joint patentees are not partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One joint inventor cannot abandon the invention to the public; date of conception, evidence of co-operation, and interference rules govern rights; joint and several inventions may be joined in same patent in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of inventions in a single patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Joinder of inventions in the same patent is theoretically incorrect but often permitted; rules of courts and Patent Office differ; Patent Office determines when joinder allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventions of different persons generally not joinable; may be joined when capable of common use or mutually dependent; aggregations cannot be joined; doubt resolved in favor of applicant; misjoinder may be cured by disclaimer or re-issue in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity, equivalence, and scope of patented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity exists when the same means produces the same effect — identity of effect, function, and means; equivalence, specific difference, and generic difference determine whether inventions are identical or diverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity depends on identity of force, object, and mode of application; absent if one cannot be substituted for another; whether same functions performed in same way; scope of patented inventions is determined by the claims; form and embodiment differences do not necessarily defeat identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment and prior use defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention not patented and abandoned to the public is not patentable; once abandoned it cannot be recalled; prior use must be complete and practical to defeat novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment while application lies unfiled may be treated differently; delays, public disclosure, and forgotten uses affect whether prior use counts for priority or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters-patent — nature, grant, and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-patent define and create the patent privilege; governed by statute and Patent Office rules; grant is a judgment that statutory prerequisites are fulfilled; must accurately disclose and define the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form, contents, signatures, recording and delivery rules; patent takes effect when issued and often relates back to application date; patents are public records and copies are evidence; grant need not recite all prerequisites but is treated as prima facie proof of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment, corrections, and re-issue of patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents may be amended or corrected by the Patent Office in the United States for clerical errors and under re-issue for certain defects; errors of substance are treated differently than clerical errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power to amend is to correspond the patent to the invention, not to change the invention or patentee; right to correct may be lost by delay; corrections should not affect intervening rights; disclaimers and re-issues are mechanisms to cure some defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent monopoly and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent privilege creates an exclusive right (monopoly) to use the invention; patent law aims to promote public interest by encouraging disclosure and invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate disclosure important to the public; patent privilege is a reward but also obligates inventor to disclose best form; public rights under natural law are recognized alongside statutory monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: License — nature, scope, and legal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is anything less than assignment and may transfer rights to make, use, or sell; distinguished from assignment, may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and does not itself transfer the monopoly unless expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License character indicated by grant words, reservations, or covenants; governed by State law; may be express or implied; written licenses merge prior parol agreements; restrictions in license (to place, extent, purpose) are enforceable and violation may be infringement; exclusive licenses have different effects and may be invaded by licensor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments, transfers, and recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights and letters-patent may be assigned or transferred; assignee may obtain a patent; the right to obtain a patent may be assigned and disposed of by will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments should be recorded; effect on licenses and subsequent transfers important; assignee's rights and defences depend on prior conveyances and notice; transfers may affect priority and rights against third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgments in patent litigation — weight and preclusive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments are conclusive on questions decided between the same parties and privies but not res judicata unless parties and issues are the same; weight of judgments as evidence of validity varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments sustaining patents do not ratify defects; weight affected by changes in law, collusion, interlocutory nature; judgments bind parties/privies and have varying precedential effect depending on court level and issues decided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction rules in patent suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of jurisdiction are not changed by Patent Law; jurisdiction over infringement suits depends on venue and personal jurisdiction rules; local jurisdiction is not conferred by mere existence of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections to jurisdiction must be timely raised; federal and state court roles differ; jurisdiction over joint infringers and foreign/domestic corporations has particular rules; lack of jurisdiction may be pleaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof and evidence of inventive act and priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive act, its date, and priority must be proved by evidence; averments in bills and evidence such as publication, use, and reduction to practice are central to proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes prior use, publication, oaths, experiments, lab notes; date of inventive act and reduction to practice is a question of fact; courts may take judicial notice of lack of inventive skill in some circumstances.
